title: Indie game development with AI
excerpt: AI made creating games faster and easier. Yet, making a good game is still hard. This is my answer to the question "If AI implements everything, what's left for me?". Turns out, quite a lot, still.

I recently built two full games with AI:

  • Inkline Town, a 3D town builder drawn in ink
  • Spirit Call, a 3D top-down shooter

I did not write a line of code. I did not read one either.

Loading interactive example…

My "game editor" was a chat, a link to playtest the game, and a web page with previews of 3D models. My "work" was sending text and screenshots. Nothing else.

And still, making those games has been hard and intense. Like never before. For weeks.

AI made writing a game faster and easier. It did not make it easy.

I really enjoy game development. Like, a lot. But game dev is intense, time-consuming, and often has a bad financial return. So much so that I wrote a full essay about my frustration.

But AI changed everything!

A project that used to take months is now a weekend of prompting, and I wanted to see if that holds for a complete game, not just a slop demo.

My goal was getting an answer to the question all game devs are asking themselves:

If AI implements everything, what's left for me?

I found the answer: The hard part didn't go away, it moved. Away from implementation, and into the choices only you can make: what game, what style, what is fun, what is broken.

AI frees your time, so you can think about the core of your game. And that's hard, and now it's all you have to do, all the time. No coding break.

Loading interactive example…

Great. Well, what does this mean, in practice, for you?

Here are all the steps I will take for my next game, everything that I learned, and how you can steal all of it.

Choosing your game is choosing your bottleneck

The first decision is yours, and it will always be so: "What game do I want to make?"

The answer you choose has the potential to make or break you and your game. Literally.

Any step in your pipeline the AI can't do becomes your full-time job.

Loading interactive example…

So when you pick a genre and a style, you are also picking where your time will go. Agents go fast, so whatever still needs you becomes the bottleneck. Make sure that step is one worth your time: taste, fun, playtest.

The characters the agent couldn't make

My plan for Spirit Call was a game like Genshin Impact (原神), with a new character every few weeks.

I played Genshin (a lot), and I got fascinated by the characters and their unique designs. Since I am also an illustrator (in training), my initial goal was to design and draw my own characters (zero AI), and having them come to life in a game.

But working on a full game with 3D models would take away all my time, leaving none for illustration.

That's where AI enters the story.

The question became: can the agent turn my designs into high-quality characters, without me stepping in? And, spoiler, the answer was no (after two days of attempts).

Simple stylized models worked well. Detailed anime characters failed every time.

I tried every route I could think of: reference sheets, prebuilt models, a full studio-style pipeline, even copying a character from another game. The results were bad, and worse, never repeatable. And all of this before animation.

Loading interactive example…

I could have done the anime characters by hand (maybe). Even with AI support, one decent character would have taken me weeks.

So I changed the style instead of the game: from full anime characters to simple stylized spirits. Not the initial vision, but one I could ship, fast, with AI in every step of the pipeline.

Even the simple spirits would have cost more by hand than the whole game took: about a month for all ten, against three weeks for all of Spirit Call. With the agent, they took about 20 minutes each:

  1. 2D design from ChatGPT
  2. Low-poly version of the design, again from ChatGPT
  3. Breakdown of every view for 3D modeling, still ChatGPT
  4. 3D modeling with Blender MCP

They were also far easier to animate. Each enemy went through the same steps.

Loading interactive example…

A style the agent can repeat

I learned my lesson with my second game, Inkline Town: an ink style, assets made by an agent, with a repeatable pipeline from day one.

Agents are not yet good at anything that requires taste: character design, detailed 3D models, animation, story. Any of it adds more work for you, personally.

If you want an agent-first fast loop, your role should only be playtesting and taste. Anything else, and the loop is broken.

Build a system that verifies for you

You should not need to read the code. The agent can handle it all. But you need layers of verification on top to make the output reliable. It starts with structure.

Entity Component System (ECS)

I use an Entity Component System (ECS): every object in the game is an entity, a bag of data (components) like position, velocity or health. Each piece of logic (a system) declares which components it reads and writes, and runs on every entity that has them.

Systems never call each other. That's what makes the architecture composable: the agent can add or rewrite one system without touching the rest, and since every system declares what it touches, the checks have something concrete to verify.

Spawn a Projectile below: it has a position and a velocity, so the same Move system that moves the player moves it too. No new code.

Loading interactive example…

Below is the same rule on a real frame of Spirit Call. The spirit, every enemy and every bolt in flight are entities: pick components, and every entity that has all of them lights up. That is how a system finds what to run on.

Automatic checks for agents

On top of that structure, you layer automatic checks. Each one takes a set of bugs off your mind:

  • Types: a wrong call doesn't compile, and the error tells the agent how to fix it. That's usually the first layer of checks
  • Headless tests and simulation: the game runs as numbers and text, no graphics. The agent can play thousands of frames and verify behavior without you
  • Lints: rules that catch the mistakes an agent keeps repeating. When the same thing breaks twice, ask for a lint
  • Every bug becomes a test: once fixed, it can't come back silently in the same form
  • Recorded playtests: the game records what happens while you play. Your session becomes data the agent can read
  • Debug sessions: the agent asks why a value changed and gets an answer, instead of guessing

The checks run between my prompt and my next playtest: the agent sees the failures, fixes them, and I never hear about most of them.

You can get creative with checks, depending on your game. In Spirit Call, I made the agent write a balance model to mathematically prove that clearing each main quest once pays for leveling a character up to the next one, without grinding.

Drag the sliders: cut the quest rewards or make level-ups pricier, and see which quest first needs replays to afford.

Loading interactive example…

None of these is mandatory. But the more of them you add (where they make sense for your game), the faster you iterate, and the more of your attention goes to taste instead of code and bugs.

You still need to know what each layer protects you from, even without knowing the implementation details. That's what lets you direct the agent when something keeps going wrong.

I created Ritmo for this exact purpose: a TypeScript ECS runtime I built in parallel with the two games, to collect all the checks in one place.

But the principles work with any engine.

Loading interactive example…

Below is a real session: my prompt, the agent's thinking, and how Ritmo helped:

The first playable is fast, the game is not

With all of that in place, the first version of your game loop comes quickly. Days, sometimes hours. Then the real work starts.

Everything that comes later, an AI cannot do alone:

  • Is the game fun and balanced to play for longer sessions?
  • Is the style clear and visually appealing?
  • Would a player understand how to play?
  • Are the assets and animations satisfying?
  • Is the story appealing?

Three quarters of Inkline Town's commits came after the first two days, when the game was already playable.

How a game with agents gets made

The start was fast. I found a style reference on X, a short video, and asked the agent to recreate it, animations included: five minutes.

Then I asked the agent to turn it into a town simulation with a few basic buildings: working ten minutes later. The core of the game took about 20 minutes. Defining the buildings and a few mechanics came next. All of that fit in the first two days.

The screenshots from those days show it: a playable town within the first hour, and a real-looking one by the evening.

Two days for something playable, then six more for content, fun and balance.

Just check Inkline Town's own commits. From day two on, most of them tune something after a play session instead of building something new: nearly two thirds of all game commits.

Loading interactive example…

The agent implements each of those changes in minutes. What takes time is figuring out what to implement: which mechanic is missing, why a system is boring, what a new player doesn't get.

Every round of that loop needs me: play, notice, decide, ask, play again.

Playtest as a player, report as a player

I never touched a number in Inkline Town. To this day, I don't know how they're computed or how they move: I only ever saw the game.

I play for around 45 minutes, as a player. Then I report what I see:

  • a strategy that dominates every other one
  • an exploit that breaks the economy
  • a moment where I didn't know what to do
  • a mechanic the game clearly needs and doesn't have

The problem of the fishery

Inkline Town's clearest case was food.

The town eats fish or bread. A fishery is one building; bread needs three buildings, all running. So I built fisheries, side by side on the same lake, and food stopped being a problem. Everyone was living on fish; bread had no reason to exist.

My bots had been playing the economy since the first day, and none of them noticed this bug.

An agent has no sense of balance: a strategy that makes the rest of the game pointless looks like any other strategy to it.

So I spoke the prompt below to the agent, as any human playtester would.

Loading interactive example…

The agent turns that into a fix, and then proves it, often with an automated economy simulation. And now that my playtests are recorded, it also has the exact numbers of the session I just played.

Checking the economy with math

For the fisheries, the fix started with a model, not a number.

I knew that if one hole like this had slipped through, there were others, and that an economy like this can be checked with math: an agent can write that check as a test.

So I asked for an economy model that weighs every number in the game against the others.

It confirmed the fishery, and showed it wasn't alone: twelve rules of the economy were broken. Finding the issues took most of the time; fixing them was fast and easy.

The problems that broke the economy never came back, because for each one we added the assumption behind it to the model. What still needed my playtests was the kind of choices I wanted the player to face.

Getting from the ledger to the fix took the agent under an hour. My part was the 45-minute match, the report, and knowing to ask for the model.

How to trust code you never read

Some of the agent's work takes hours. I don't watch it. I don't review it.

When it's done, the checks have already run. Types compile, tests pass, lints are clean, simulations hold. Implementation is verified before it reaches me, against what the checks encode.

Loading interactive example…

What the checks miss

Passing the checks doesn't mean the game is ready. What reaches me is what they miss: a side panel hiding a button, an unclear tutorial line, a mechanic that works exactly as specified but isn't fun.

Simple but glaring example: an empty side panel covering half the map. I sent the screenshot; half an hour and multiple iterations later, it was fixed.

Then I open the game (never the code) and restart it from the very beginning to judge what no check measures: whether it's fun.

Since I never know what the agent changed, every time I open the game I meet it fresh, like a new player: I read the UI for the first time and follow the tutorial step by step.

My reports mention what felt off and why, never how to fix it. My sessions are recorded, so the agent can replay my actions, take its own screenshots, and see the issue.

Bots are not players

You can even create various bot profiles, each with different skills, as a check to balance the game:

The bots show which quests can be cleared, and catch it when a change breaks one. They don't tell you how many players would clear them, or whether it's fun.

Know the tools underneath

The checks are only as good as the rules behind them. When one keeps failing, you need to tell whether the agent got it wrong or a rule is missing, and for that you need to know the tools underneath.

My trust came from the stack: my own engine plus Effect, which I know well enough to let the agent run.

If you're not into development or math, expect to hit a wall at some point.

Remember the fisheries: there, the wall was knowing to ask for a math model. Without that, you would be stuck in a much longer loop, fixing each case by hand from playtests.

Your contribution was never the code

If you have been building your game by hand for years, I know you are screaming: "But it stops being my game if I don't write any of it!"

It doesn't. Your contribution was never the code. It was the ideas, the feel, the hundreds of small decisions about what's fun. That is exactly the part AI can't do, and the part that now gets all your time.

Loading interactive example…

If you enjoy writing every line, keep doing it. But if you want to make and sell games, building by hand means years on a game you're not sure will work, while an agent writes a full system in minutes, and the models keep getting better.

My prediction: on average, games made with an AI system will ship faster and sell better.

Not because AI makes better games, but because the time no longer spent on code goes into playtesting, fun, and the bugs only a human catches. If you keep writing code, you simply don't have enough resources for all of it.

If you want to make a game, here is the order:

  1. Pick your game and style with the bottleneck in mind: test early that the AI can produce what you need
  2. Build verification alongside the first playable: start with types, lints and tests for the core rules, whatever your engine. Add headless simulations and math models of your numbers as playtests show what needs protecting. Ritmo has them all built in, but it isn't required
  3. Verify that the core gameplay is fun, early: and expect most of the work to come after it
  4. Playtest as a player, report what's broken, let the agent fix and prove it: repeat. Ask for what the player would notice, never for code

Loading interactive example…

It's still hard. It's faster. And, if you ask me, way more fun than before.

Why more fun? Because my time goes to the part I care about. Since code doesn't matter much, the focus is all on gameplay and game feel. I am playing more instead of bothering with code details.

And the final game is still mine, something that no agent alone could make.

What changed
